source.title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: In causal supervised learning, can the field develop standardized, targeted benchmarks for invariance learning so practitioners can compare methods on shared tasks that deliberately vary spurious associations between training and test environments instead of relying on ad hoc toy experiments?

evidence.quote:
Previous works in invariance learning often evaluate their suggested methods on
novel toy experiments instead of a standardized test bed. As a result, practitioners
cannot quickly determine the best approach for their problem.

accepted.question_text: How can causal assumptions and invariance-learning ideas be used to improve adversarial robustness and meta-learning, for example by treating robustness as invariance to perturbations and by learning task-invariant structure or interventions over task variables?

evidence.quote:
We note two active ML research areas akin to invariance learning: adversarial ro-
bustness and meta-learning. We put forward to investigate how causal assumptions
may beneﬁt these areas, as it is currently underexplored.

accepted.question_text: For invariant feature learning, which additional supervision signals beyond labels are most useful, including combinations of content-invariant transformations, multi-environment data, high-dimensional environment descriptions, and richer object or attribute labels, and how should such signals be exploited to separate interventions on spurious features?

evidence.quote:
Identifying and exploiting other forms of labels that
inform invariant feature learning is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: In causal representation learning, what level of abstraction should the latent causal variables use, and what specifications or supervisory signals are necessary, sufficient, or relaxable for identifying a useful structural causal model over latent generative factors rather than over overly fine-grained or overly coarse variables?

evidence.quote:
Thus, what kinds of supervisory signals are optimal for CRL, what trade-oﬀs exist,
and which signals are reasonable to require, are all open problems.

accepted.question_text: How can structural assignment learning in causal generative modeling scale to substantially larger causal graphs while still supporting flexible counterfactual sample generation, given that existing methods either work on low-order graphs or rely on amortized structural assignments over only a limited set of plausible interventions?

evidence.quote:
Hence, how
to tackle the scalability of the underlying causal graphs in structural assignment
learning remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: When, and by how much, does counterfactual data augmentation generated by causal generative models improve generalization relative to non-counterfactual or hand-crafted augmentations, and can such augmentation effectiveness also serve as a benchmark for comparing causal generative methods?

evidence.quote:
Exploring when and by how much CFDA using causal generative models improves
generalization remains an open problem.
Such a benchmarking method is under-explored.

accepted.question_text: How can causal feature-attribution methods and contrastive explanation methods be unified so an explanation identifies not only which changes would achieve a desired outcome but also which features should remain unchanged, yielding a more complete and actionable explanation of a model decision?

evidence.quote:
Attribution and explanation methods can be complementary. For example, as Verma
et al. [132] point out that explanations need to emphasize what should remain the
same in additionto what should change in order to achieve a desired outcome.

accepted.question_text: How can causal explanation methods be made scalable enough for large systems with many features and many users, despite exact attribution methods becoming computationally intractable and contrastive explanation methods becoming hard because of plausibility and actionability constraints?

evidence.quote:
To make explanations deployable in large-scale systems with many users, approxi-
mate methods are highly needed.

accepted.question_text: How should causal explanation methods handle dynamics such as distribution shift, model updates, and changing utility functions, so that explanations remain valid over time instead of assuming a fixed black-box model in a static environment?

evidence.quote:
Most explanation methods assume a static black-box model that does not change
over time.

Naturally, these issues arise
for model explanations too, and there exists only limited work to address them
[165, 166, 167].

accepted.question_text: How can deployed causal explanation systems be made secure and privacy-preserving against attacks such as model extraction, decision-boundary recovery, membership inference, and extraction of causal knowledge from repeated explanation queries?

evidence.quote:
There has been very limited work on guarding explanation methods against such
concerns.

accepted.question_text: Given the impossibility result that no attribution method can always be both continuous under small input changes and recourse sensitive for every utility notion and model, what workaround or reformulation can preserve useful robustness and actionable recourse at the same time?

evidence.quote:
Future
work should therefore consider workarounds to circumvent Fokkema et al. [162]’s
impossibility result.

accepted.question_text: In causal fairness, how can equity or harm-based notions be operationalized as alternatives to equality-based fairness definitions, and how would such criteria complement or conflict with existing fairness notions used in machine learning?

evidence.quote:
An exciting future direc-
tion is to operationalize this deﬁnition and examine how it enhances or contradicts
existing deﬁnitions of fairness [3].

accepted.question_text: How should fairness be defined and evaluated beyond predictive outputs, especially for recourse systems and causal algorithmic recourse, including whether recourse opportunities and intervention policies are fairly distributed across protected and unprotected groups?

evidence.quote:
For example, the question
of whether it is appropriate to perform societal interventions on all individuals in
a subgroup.

accepted.question_text: When causal fairness quantities, especially counterfactuals, are only partially identifiable, how should sensitivity analysis and realistic simulation be used to assess fairness methods and to understand how violations of identification assumptions affect fairness estimation?

evidence.quote:
While previous
causal fairness work has partly addressed these issues [175, 178, 195], we foresee
more important work to be done in sensitivity analysis through realistic simulations

accepted.question_text: Do social categories such as race and gender admit meaningful interventions or counterfactual manipulation in causal fairness models, and if not, what kinds of causal or non-interventionist formalisms should replace variable-based DAG treatments of those categories?

evidence.quote:
More broadly, Kasirzadeh
and Smart [199] review various papers at this intersection between sociology and
causal modeling, concluding that social categories often do not admit counterfactual
manipulation.

accepted.question_text: When multiple causal fairness criteria conflict and cannot all be satisfied simultaneously, how should practitioners characterize, optimize, and govern the trade-offs among admissible criteria without producing policies that every stakeholder would reject?

evidence.quote:
Hence, in practice, the trade-oﬀ between multiple
admissible criteria has to be balanced.

accepted.question_text: Under what conditions can a trained model produce unfair predictions even when the training labels themselves are fair, and how can causal fairness methods detect, rule out, or stress-test such introduced unfairness?

evidence.quote:
Minimal work exists investigating when fair training labels may not yield a fair
model.

Future research may stress-test
the validity of the in this section introduced fairness criteria.

accepted.question_text: Can causal reinforcement learning adopt unified evaluation environments so methods with the same goal, such as learning environment transition dynamics for better sample efficiency, can be compared on overlapping tasks instead of on incompatible bespoke benchmarks?

evidence.quote:
Lack of uniﬁed evaluation environments: For example, in causal model-based RL,
all methods share the same goal of learning the environment transition dynamics
(e.g., to improve sample eﬃciency for policy search). However, there is no overlap in
their evaluation environments.

accepted.question_text: Can the many partially overlapping causal and non-causal reinforcement-learning formalisms for shared-dynamics, partially observed, or confounded environments be compared rigorously and possibly unified so practitioners are not forced to choose among redundant formulations with unclear relationships?

evidence.quote:
We suggest that fu-
ture work compares the applicability of diﬀerent formalisms more rigorously and
possibly uniﬁes them.

accepted.question_text: How can purely offline reinforcement learning deconfound observational datasets when the behavior policy and environment are unobserved, so policies learned from logged data are less biased by hidden confounding?

evidence.quote:
We believe that deconfounding observa-
tional data is under-explored in pure oﬄine RL settings, and only a few works have
addressed this setup [256].

accepted.question_text: How can reinforcement-learning agents be designed to make decisions using counterfactual reasoning, despite the difficulty of learning correct structural causal models, and when does such counterfactual decision-making provide practical gains such as reduced policy-search bias, better multi-agent credit assignment, or better human-in-the-loop reasoning?

evidence.quote:
Bareinboim [213] expose that inference of coun-
terfactuals is neglected in the RL literature, possibly due to the diﬃculty of learning
correct SCMs.

We hope to see more carefully-designed counterfactual agents for
real-world systems that may take inspiration from Bottou et al. [208].
